name: Fools and Roads
description: They say that Berland has exactly two problems, fools and roads. Besides, Berland has n cities, populated by the fools and connected by the roads. All Berland roads are bidirectional. As there are many fools in Berland, between each pair of cities there is a path (or else the fools would get upset). Also, between each pair of cities there is no more than one simple path (or else the fools would get lost). But that is not the end of Berland's special features. In this country fools sometimes visit each other and thus spoil the roads. The fools aren't very smart, so they always use only the simple paths. A simple path is the path which goes through every Berland city not more than once. The Berland government knows the paths which the fools use. Help the government count for each road, how many distinct fools can go on it. Note how the fools' paths are given in the input.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer n ( 2 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ) — the number of cities. Each of the next n - 1 lines contains two space-separated integers u i , v i ( 1 ≤ u i , v i ≤ n , u i ≠ v i ), that means that there is a road connecting cities u i and v i . The next line contains integer k ( 0 ≤ k ≤ 10 5 ) — the number of pairs of fools who visit each other. Next k lines contain two space-separated numbers. The i -th line ( i > 0) contains numbers a i , b i ( 1 ≤ a i , b i ≤ n ). That means that the fool number 2 i - 1 lives in city a i and visits the fool number 2 i , who lives in city b i . The given pairs describe simple paths, because between every pair of cities there is only one simple path.
output_specification: Print n - 1 integer. The integers should be separated by spaces. The i -th number should equal the number of fools who can go on the i -th road. The roads are numbered starting from one in the order, in which they occur in the input.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 191C — Fools and Roads [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
